title: Auto Focus
full_review:
"Auto Focus" (Sony Classics) follows the steady demise of TV sitcom star Bob Crane, whose gleeful promiscuity ended only when he was murdered in 1978.

The movie strongly implies that the murderer was Crane's eager partner in nightly hunts for fresh female flesh, but that suspect was acquitted and the crime is still on the books. Unfortunately, director Paul Schrader's shallow biopic seems more visually interested in reveling in the two men's nightly conquests than in being a cautionary tale with any insights to
offer.

In 1964, Catholic family man Crane (Greg Kinnear) was a Los Angeles disc jockey urging his agent (a poignant Ron Liebman) to get him dramatic acting roles. His skyrocket to fame came with the title role in the 1965-71 sitcom "Hogan's Heroes." Wife Anne (Rita Wilson) was concerned about his collection of dirty magazines, but once he became a celebrity Crane found he could have his pick of beautiful women willing to actually sleep with him.

Although Crane seeks out his parish priest regarding his temptations, he instead quickly turns into a sex addict. Crane is lured into these one-night stands by technician John "Carpy" Carpenter (Willem Dafoe), who shares an interest in girlie photography and videotaping their sexual conquests.

Soon they are hosting nightly orgies. When Anne comes across his stash of photos of him copulating with countless females she leaves with their three children. Since Crane was already having an affair with series co-star Patricia (Maria Bello) -- who claims she doesn't mind his constant philandering -- he makes her the second Mrs. Crane.

After the sitcom is canceled and word gets around Hollywood about Crane's decadence he's reduced to acting in on-the-road dinner theater. Yet he and Carpy see this as an opportunity to meet and seduce new babes every night. A second divorce is just another rung on a self-destructive spiral that culminates when Crane is found bludgeoned to death by his own camera equipment.

What would have made this movie compelling -- an incisive character study -- is sorely lacking. But the filmmaker never takes us below the surface of the two leads' extremely tawdry lifestyle. Dafoe certainly gives an appropriately creepy performance, but he seems to exist in a vacuum. It's as if he has no identity whatever except as a hanger-on to celebrity Crane, who can attract the women for them to use and cast aside with impunity. He is pathetic, unchanging and never for a moment seems to give any thought to his objectification of women and his embrace of hedonism.

Crane as well is initially seen as a decent family guy but once he rejects his priest's advice he dives wholeheartedly into compulsive adultery, and his claim at the end to Carpy that he intends to cool their relationship and lay off sex for a while (giving angry Carpy a motive for murder) sounds completely unconvincing.

So, in essence, you have a movie that focuses on their nights (and years) of constant orgies where love would definitely be an unwelcome incursion on their lust-filled rampages. The two men are also seen together watching a tape of themselves in action while it's clearly implied they are masturbating. The women seen are a sorry assemblage, indeed, so lacking in self-esteem they will allow themselves to be utterly demeaned just to be with someone famous.

As if there is not enough graphic sexual imagery, another gratuitous scene shows Crane's fantasy of his topless lover being pawed by a series co-star while his first wife and children watch. Neither man ever seems to regret for a moment how they have exploited women, as sex is seen as only about male gratification.

Although the film doesn't go as far as to celebrate their sexual addictions as something terrific, it never goes beyond chronicling how great Crane and Carpy thought such a sick lifestyle was, no matter the human consequences. By showing so much skin but never going beyond skin-deep analysis, the unsatisfying film leaves viewers at a loss as to why Crane chose to lose the respect of his peers, his career and his family.

Due to many promiscuous sexual encounters with full female nudity, implied masturbation, brief violence, fleeting drug abuse and frequent rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. (2002)
